title: Olympic Torches: Remember Those?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and design of the Olympic torch. They trace the torch relay to ancient Greece and the Prometheus myth, the sacred flame at Hera's altar in Olympia, and its revival by Carl Diem for the 1936 Berlin Games, plus the first Winter Olympic relays (Norway in 1952, Innsbruck 1964, Squaw Valley 1960). They cover modern torch design (the 1960 Squaw Valley torch by Disney designer John Hinch, propane/butane fuel, redundant pilot flames, lightweight construction, deliberate deactivation after use, and sustainability materials such as Tokyo 2020's aluminum from temporary housing). They discuss fuel history (gunpowder, olive oil, hexamine, naphtha, magnesium/aluminum), torch collector prices, unusual relays (robot Hubo in PyeongChang 2018, Montreal 1976 satellite relay, space and underwater legs), and famous lighting moments (Muhammad Ali in Atlanta 1996, Antonio Rebollo in Barcelona 1992, the 1964 Tokyo dove incident). The episode ends with a listener mail segment about wasp removal.

segments.title: Book plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh plugs the new book Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things, then the hosts banter about the postponed Tokyo Olympics and coronavirus, and introduce the episode on Olympic torches.

segments.title: Ancient Greek origins of the torch
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Prometheus myth of stolen fire and the Greek torch relays. They cover the Olympic truce, the sacred flame at Hera's altar in Olympia lit with a parabolic mirror, and the flame's continuation through the ancient Games.

segments.title: Revival of the torch relay: Amsterdam, Berlin and Winter Games
segments.summary: Pierre de Coubertin revived the Games without a torch relay. Amsterdam 1928 had a burning cauldron but no relay. Carl Diem introduced the relay for Berlin 1936, which the Nazis used for legitimacy, and the torch had no swastika. The Winter relay began in 1952 in Norway, honoring Sondre Norheim, and moved to Olympia-origin relays in 1964 at Innsbruck. Squaw Valley 1960 was also lit in Norway.

segments.title: Torch design, weight, and deactivation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the design process and RFP for the London 2012 torch, the need for a light, reliable, and ergonomic torch, and the 1960 Squaw Valley torch by Disney designer John Hinch that set the modern template. Torches use liquid fuel that becomes gas under pressure, like a camp stove, with redundant pilot flames. Torches are deliberately disabled after use, and an Atlanta torch repair website is mentioned.

segments.title: Torch collecting, prices, and sustainability
segments.summary: The hosts describe torch buyback and sale to the public, with prices near cost for Tokyo's torch, and collector prices for older torches including a record for the 1952 Helsinki torch. They discuss Mexico City 1968's torch as the longest-burning and sustainability in Tokyo 2020 torch made from temporary housing aluminum after the Fukushima disaster.

segments.title: Fuel history, unusual relays, and famous lightings
segments.summary: The hosts review past torch fuels (gunpowder, olive oil, hexamine, naphtha), now propane and butane. They discuss unusual relays such as the robot Hubo in PyeongChang 2018, Montreal 1976 satellite relay, space and underwater legs. They recall famous cauldron lightings: Muhammad Ali at Atlanta 1996, Antonio Rebollo at Barcelona 1992, and the doves at Tokyo 1964.

segments.title: Listener mail on wasp removal
segments.summary: A listener criticizes the hosts' earlier wasp episode for assuming listeners can hire professionals to remove nests. Chuck describes trapping a wasp under a bowl and screen to release it outdoors.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give the email contact and sign off.
